content: An elective cesarean section refers to a cesarean delivery performed on a pregnant woman who is not in labor. This procedure is carried out either due to a medical or obstetrical indication identified before labor begins or at the explicit request of the pregnant patient. Elective cesarean sections are also referred to as planned cesarean sections. In contrast, a cesarean section performed during labor out of necessity is termed an emergency cesarean section. When a medical or obstetrical reason for cesarean delivery is identified during pregnancy but before the onset of labor, physicians often schedule the procedure at a predetermined time rather than waiting for labor to begin. These planned cesarean sections are performed for various reasons, including repeat cesarean sections, placenta previa, abnormal fetal presentations, multiple pregnancies, known labor obstructions, and maternal medical conditions such as heart disease. The advantages of scheduling the delivery include the ability to utilize daytime services when staffing and access to resources are optimal, as well as allowing both the patient and her family, as well as the healthcare team, to plan and prepare adequately. However, there are risks associated with this approach. If the timing of the cesarean section is set too early, the baby may be delivered prematurely or face complications. Prenatal testing is typically employed to minimize this risk. Critics of elective cesarean sections argue that the indications for the procedure are sometimes too lenient, that a trial of labor could have been successful in many cases, and that physicians and institutions may inappropriately benefit by reducing nighttime and weekend work, potentially at the expense of the patient undergoing an unnecessary procedure or the baby missing the benefits of natural delivery. Additionally, the fear of litigation is often cited as a factor driving higher rates of elective cesarean sections. While many women who have had a previous cesarean section can avoid a repeat procedure by attempting vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC), some argue that this approach carries an increased risk of uterine rupture. In recent years, cesarean sections have increasingly been performed at the request of the patient, even in the absence of medical or obstetrical necessity. This practice is sometimes referred to as cesarean delivery on maternal request or planned elective cesarean section. As of 2006, there is no specific ICD code for this indication, making it difficult to determine the prevalence of such requests. Importantly, the mother is the only individual who may request this intervention without a medical or obstetrical indication.
